newsitem.title: THAILAND: Tokyo loan pledge fails to spur Thai markets.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo loan pledge fails to spur Thai markets.

text.p: A $16 billion pledge for an international rescue package for financially strapped Thailand failed to lift the baht or rally sluggish Thai stocks on Monday.

Dealers and brokers said the loan package, spearheaded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Japan, failed to boost sentiment for the Thai economy hammered this year by the collapse of the finance and property sectors.

"People harbour doubts whether outside aid could produce a quick economic recovery at a time that we see many other problems. The baht outlook does not improve as long as capital still refuses to flow back," said Prateep Leelakittikul of Hongkong and Shanghai Bank.
The baht held steady at 31.300/31.480 to the dollar on late Monday afternoon. The composite SET Index finished down 4.60 points, or 0.72 percent, at 632.25.
Analysts also attributed sluggish trading on the baht and Thai stocks to a holiday mood as equities and financial markets would be closed on Tuesday for Queen Sirikit's birthday.

They said they were unimpressed by a decision of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's government to cut its 1997/1998 (October-September) budget by 50-70 billion baht ($1.6-2.3 billion) to offset an expected decline in tax revenue.
Chavalit said on Monday his cabinet would review details of the proposed budget cut next week. He did not elaborate, but said spending on education and health would be least affected.

The opposition has called on the government to slash the 1997/1998 budget of 982 billion baht by at least 100 billion baht, a figure that they said would help Chavalit avoid his unpopular decision to raise Thailand's value added tax (VAT).

Thailand last week announced a three percentage point VAT hike from August 16 as part of tough austerity measures taken on the advice of the IMF to revive the battered economy which is growing at its slowest in over a decade.

Jacqueline Ong of I.D.E.A. in Singapore said the IMF-sponsored loan package produced little market reaction. She said currency dealers would reassess Thailand's fundamentals after mid-August when forward three-month baht/dollar contracts taken by speculators in May were due to mature.
She said the muted market response to the Tokyo package was also due to a further setback for the Malaysian ringgit which hit a new 42-month low on Monday.

"Even the positive Singapore announcement of its gross domestic product growth did not help much," Ong said, referring to Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's projection on Friday that the Singapore GDP was expected to expand six to seven percent this year.
The analyst said, however, that she saw a limited downside for Thai stocks after their 24 percent loss this year.
